textArea.b: Our riskiest claim, and its test
A practice pays $500 per cardiologist a year despite free intake tools.

g.textArea: Slide 7 of the Maker Day 2 deck, word for word; backup A3 shortens it to "a practice pays $500 per cardiologist a year". 0 of 21 logged interviews were practice managers (and 0 were cardiologists or relatives).

Test by Oct 23: 5 practice-manager conversations with a one-page price card. Pass = 3 of 5 name the budget owner and accept $500/yr in principle, and 1 signs a non-binding letter of intent naming a target start month. The paid letter follows once we have a company, a BAA template and insurance.

Price card ($500/yr and $99/mo) to 5 independent NYC practice managers. Ask: "Show us your new-patient form and your EHR check-in. Does either ask which side, which relative, what age?"; minutes spent on family history; new patients per cardiologist per month, by payer; which EHR; who approves a purchase

textArea.b: Why this is the riskiest claim

g.textArea:
• Step 4.4, unproven #1: A practice pays $500 per cardiologist a year despite free intake tools (no buyer interviews, letters or pilots).
• Step 4 (deck A3): saved staff time only breaks even at $500 a year, so FamGenix's $500-a-year clinician license [111] sets our price; the pilot has to show time saved or clinical value.
• Step 3: The old parts lower the risk of the business model but also mean the buyer already has cheap substitutes, which is why price is the riskiest assumption.
• Configuration: The weak joint is the same in every box: no practice has said it will pay.
• Step 5 verdict: The main risk is price, not technology.
• If it fails: fewer than 3 of 5 cardiology managers naming a budget owner by Oct 23 means we run the same five calls with primary care practice managers (see the Wedge frame).
